title: Enrichment and Evolution Mechanism of Lithium in the Intercrystalline Brine of the Balun Mahai Basin, Qaidam Basin
content:
This study classified intercrystalline brine samples into three clusters using self-organizing maps (SOM), with lithium concentrations exhibiting a pattern of high values in the north and low values in the south and southwest. Lithium isotope provides a basis for identifying the source of lithium in intercrystalline brine.


ABSTRACT

Intercrystalline brine is an important type of lithium-bearing resource. However, the spatial heterogeneity of Li concentrations and the geochemical processes controlling their distribution in highly mineralized intercrystalline brine remain poorly understood. This study classified intercrystalline brine samples collected from the Balun Mahai Basin (BLMH) into three clusters using self-organizing maps (SOM). On this basis, multiple isotopes (δ18O, δD and δ7Li) and hydrochemical analyses and ionic ratios were used to characterize the spatial distribution characteristics of Li and its potential control mechanism. The results showed that the intercrystalline brine in the study area was predominantly of the Na–Cl type, with lithium concentrations exhibiting a pattern of high values in the north and low values in the south and southwest. Geochemical evidence indicated that the spatial differentiation of lithium in the intercrystalline brine was likely the outcome of combined evaporative evolution, mineral dissolution, and deep fluid mixing. The northern high-lithium zone was primarily controlled by evaporative concentration and dissolution of evaporite minerals and was characterized by the synergistic enrichment of Li, K, and Mg. The southern low-lithium brine was markedly diluted by the mixed recharge of deep Ca–Cl type waters, accompanied by intense reverse cation exchange. These findings provided a basis for regional lithium resource exploration and evaluation, as well as for research on brine-type lithium mineralization processes.
